question: What is the main reason a doctor performs a skin biopsy?

options.A: To completely remove a large area of infected tissue
options.B: To obtain a tissue sample for microscopic examination
options.C: To drain purulent fluid from a deep subcutaneous abscess
options.D: To deliver topical medications directly to the dermis

explanation: You've got this! A skin biopsy simply means taking a tiny piece of skin so the lab can look at it closely under a microscope to figure out what's going on. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h1)

question: A patient has a stubborn rash that won't go away with standard treatment, so a skin biopsy is ordered. What is the goal?

options.A: Confirm a definitive diagnosis and guide treatment
options.B: Decontaminate the skin surface from bacterial flora
options.C: Remove all inflamed nerve endings causing itching
options.D: Prevent the rash from spreading to other body parts

explanation: When standard creams don't work, a biopsy helps pin down the exact problem so the healthcare team can choose the right medicine that actually works. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which biopsy tool uses a tiny round, cookie-cutter blade to take a full-depth core of skin?
explanation: Think of a punch biopsy like a tiny apple corer! It uses a small, hollow circular blade to get a clean sample going through all the skin layers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h2)

question: A patient has a deep, suspicious mole that needs to be completely removed with a clear border of healthy skin. Which method is best?
explanation: An excisional biopsy takes out the entire lesion plus a small safety margin of healthy skin around it—great when we need total removal, like checking for melanoma. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h2)

question: Which medication history is crucial to check before doing a skin biopsy?
explanation: Always check for blood thinners! They can make bleeding hard to stop during and after the procedure, so the team needs a heads-up. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h3)

question: A patient scheduled for a small skin biopsy is panicking because they are sure it means they have cancer. How should the nurse reply?

options.A: Confirm that the doctor strongly suspects a malignant tumor
options.B: Suggest that the patient cancel the procedure until they feel calmer
options.C: Tell the patient not to worry because skin problems are never serious
options.D: Explain that biopsies are done to check many different conditions, not just cancer

explanation: It's totally normal for patients to worry about the 'C-word.' Gently reminding them that biopsies check for simple rashes, fungus, and routine infections too can be a huge relief. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h3)

question: Why do doctors often add epinephrine to the local numbing medicine for a skin biopsy?

options.A: To constrict blood vessels and reduce bleeding
options.B: To neutralize acidic pH levels in the local tissue
options.C: To completely eliminate the initial stinging sensation
options.D: To speed up the healing time of the skin wound

explanation: Epinephrine makes blood vessels temporarily narrow (vasoconstriction), which keeps the workspace nice and clear of blood and helps the numbing medicine last longer. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why should local numbing medicine with epinephrine be avoided when doing a biopsy right on the tip of the nose?

options.A: It makes the skin too soft for the punch blade to cut
options.B: It completely stops the local anesthetic from numbing the skin
options.C: It can cause severe restricted blood flow and tissue death
options.D: It reacts poorly with standard skin antiseptic solutions

explanation: Places like the nose tip have end-arteries with no backup blood supply. Adding epinephrine there can cut off circulation completely and cause the tissue to die (necrosis). [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h4)

question: After cleaning the skin with an antiseptic and before giving the numbing injection, what is the next important step?

options.A: Suturing the edges of the anticipated wound
options.B: Placing sterile surgical drapes over the patient
options.C: Applying direct pressure to collapse blood vessels
options.D: Allowing the antiseptic solution to dry completely

explanation: Patience is key! Antiseptics need a little air-drying time to actually kill the germs before the skin barrier is opened up. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h5)

question: After a punch biopsy on the arm, a little blood keeps oozing out. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Flush the open wound with sterile hydrogen peroxide
options.B: Remove the newly placed sutures to inspect the base
options.C: Apply direct firm pressure with sterile gauze
options.D: Immediately apply a full-thickness skin graft

explanation: Simple, direct pressure with sterile gauze is your best friend for stopping minor bleeding before doing anything else. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h5)

question: How long should a patient keep their fresh biopsy bandage clean, dry, and in place?
explanation: Leaving the first bandage on for 24 to 48 hours gives the skin a chance to start forming its natural protective seal against germs. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why do we recommend putting petroleum jelly on a healing biopsy site instead of letting a hard crust form?

options.A: Ointment prevents the local anesthetic from wearing off too early
options.B: Petroleum jelly contains strong antibiotics to kill all skin bacteria
options.C: It prevents the sutures from dissolving before the skin closes
options.D: A moist environment helps new skin cells migrate and heal faster

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! Keeping the wound soft with ointment lets new skin cells slide across and close the gap much faster than when a dry, crunchy scab is in the way. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h6)

question: Which sign points strongly to a wound infection after a skin biopsy?

options.A: A thin line of pink tissue along the suture line
options.B: Temporary numbness fading after the local anesthetic wears off
options.C: Spreading redness, warmth, and purulent drainage
options.D: Mild itching around the edges of the adhesive bandage

explanation: Redness that keeps spreading, feeling hot to the touch, pus (purulent drainage), and worsening pain are classic red flags that bacteria have moved in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h7)

question: Two days after a punch biopsy, a patient calls to say there is a firm, painful, purple lump right under their stitches. What likely happened?
explanation: When blood gets trapped and pools under the closed skin, it forms a tender, purple bump called a hematoma. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h7)

question: What liquid solution is standard for preserving a skin biopsy sample on its way to the lab?
explanation: Neutral buffered formalin is the go-to liquid fixative. It stops the tissue from breaking down so the pathologist can examine the cells clearly. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h8)

question: Why is writing a detailed clinical history on the lab form so important when sending off a skin biopsy?

options.A: It determines how much money the laboratory will bill the patient's insurance
options.B: It dictates the type of suture material that should be used in the clinic
options.C: It proves to the hospital administration that the procedure was strictly necessary
options.D: It guides the pathologist on what specific features to look for under the microscope

explanation: Pathologists aren't mind readers! Giving them details like the patient's age and what the rash looked like helps them zoom in on the right clues under the microscope. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h8)
